title: AI Is Eroding the Right to Privacy
author: Daniel Solove

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Solove does not assess AI’s task-level legal capability, verification demands or effects on legal-work design. He instead redirects the deployment question toward privacy harms and regulatory safeguards, while similarly favouring context-sensitive balancing and privacy-protective redesign over blanket adoption or prohibition.
qs: The challenge is, how do we come up with a thoughtful balance so that we have technology used in ways that are helpful but that don't unduly harm us?
Maybe they could be redesigned in certain ways to protect privacy.

kp.k: Privacy doctrine has not kept pace with digital technology
kp.d: Solove argues that privacy law, especially Fourth Amendment doctrine governing government searches and surveillance, has historically provided inadequate protection against digital technologies despite some recent improvement. He attributes this partly to courts' and policymakers' narrow, antiquated conceptions of privacy. This is a scholarly assessment in an interview, not a measured finding about legal-service productivity or employment.
qs: I think the law has not generally done a good job of protecting privacy
they just have very antiquated notions of privacy, notions and ideas of privacy that I think are overly narrow and that are not really responsive to the technological world we're living in today.

kp.k: Government surveillance and commercial data collection require joint regulation
kp.d: Solove distinguishes constitutional rights against government from statutory and other protections that can also regulate companies. He argues that government access to commercially collected information makes a government-only regulatory approach ineffective. He describes government purchases of app-derived location profiles from data brokers as an attempted workaround to warrant protections, while presenting his view that Carpenter's general principle should prohibit that workaround rather than claiming the issue is settled.
qs: you can't really regulate government surveillance without regulating surveillance capitalism, without regulating the private sector and the information they have.
So we'll just buy it from a data broker. Well, I think it's the same thing.
I think if you apply the general principle of the case, the government shouldn't be able to get the information by buying it from a broker.

kp.k: Third-party doctrine creates uncertainty for digitally mediated lives
kp.d: Solove criticizes the doctrine that sharing information with third parties undermines a reasonable expectation of privacy, because digital intermediaries hold extensive records of everyday activity. He distinguishes Jones's physical tracking-device trespass rationale from Carpenter's protection for extensively collected location information. He considers Carpenter an insufficiently clear limitation, recommends abandoning the third-party doctrine, and argues that unresolved boundaries complicate police warrant decisions and enable government workarounds.
qs: with digital technologies, third parties know everything.
it should have just gotten rid of the third-party doctrine because it just doesn't make sense, it doesn't really work.
The court didn't give us a test or guidance for how to determine this.
It's tough on the police because they don't know, okay, when should we go and get a warrant?

kp.k: AI inference makes ordinary disclosures reveal sensitive information
kp.d: Solove rejects the idea that privacy matters only to people hiding wrongdoing: disclosure is contextual, and apparently ordinary information can support unexpected sensitive inferences. He uses Target's pregnancy-prediction story as an illustrative reported example, not a quantified AI study, and argues that algorithms can infer health, religion and political beliefs. Separately, responding to the host's observation about intimate chatbot disclosures, he identifies both privacy risks and potentially poor emotional-support advice.
qs: We share information in context.

we don't realize in today's age that the algorithms can look at that data, analyze that data, and then determine their religion, their political beliefs, other very sensitive information, their health.
One is the access of information, the privacy issues. There's also issues with regard to what information they're getting back.

kp.k: Privacy notices impose unrealistic burdens on technology users
kp.d: Solove argues that users neither read nor meaningfully consent to lengthy, unclear agreements, which he says lawyers draft to preserve companies' discretion. He also criticizes the asymmetry of treating contractual privacy waivers as significant while disregarding promises of privacy under third-party doctrine. Using food and vehicle safety as regulatory analogies, he advocates mandatory protections rather than requiring consumers to become technical and legal experts before using essential technologies.
qs: I don't think people agree or consent to anything. They don't even read them. They don't know what they say.
they're written by lawyers to be intentionally vague and unclear.
that's putting way too much onus on the consumer to do this.
I shouldn't have to become an AI expert to use AI.

kp.k: AI removes human bottlenecks that constrained surveillance
kp.d: Solove agrees with the host's mechanism that surveillance was previously constrained by the personnel needed to review information. He argues that automated monitoring and suspicious-pattern flagging make existing public and private camera networks more invasive by increasing analytical efficiency. He predicts pervasive audiovisual recording as cameras and wearables proliferate; the transcript provides no quantified adoption evidence or deadline for this forecast.
qs: surveillance was limited by the lack of people to parse the data.
AI algorithms can analyze the data and can flag certain patterns that are suspicious and then send those up for review.
we're going to enter an age where everything is recorded at all times, audio, video, you know, all recorded.

kp.k: Facial recognition erodes obscurity and enables targeted exclusion
kp.d: Solove argues that privacy includes practical obscurity in public, not simply secrecy: recording, aggregation and identification destroy the protection of being unnoticed. He cites work by Woodrow Hartzog and Evan Selinger on obscurity and reports the use of facial recognition to exclude lawyers involved in litigation against what he recalls as Madison Square Garden. He uses that episode to illustrate possible wider exclusion based on beliefs or purchases, rather than claiming those hypothetical practices are established.
qs: we so much have depended on and didn't appreciate the obscurity by which we go about most of our lives. And that is being lost to this technology.
There's an example where there are these lawyers who were involved in lawsuits against I believe it was the Madison Square Garden, and they kicked the lawyers out.
they used facial recognition to do that, and that could happen anywhere, right?

kp.k: Public-information exclusions and contextual torts leave protection uncertain
kp.d: Responding to surveillance and wearable-recording hypotheticals, Solove says many, but not all, privacy laws exempt publicly available information. He describes public disclosure of private facts as a possible remedy whose application depends on sensitivity, context, publicity, newsworthiness, jurisdiction and judicial interpretation. He stresses inconsistent treatment of shared secrets and public figures, rather than offering a categorical legal answer.
qs: a lot of the laws exempt publicly available information.
There is a tort that's recognized in most states called Public Disclosure of Private Facts.
there really aren't very clear, easy rules here.
it depends on what jurisdiction you're in and where are you and what the case law says and what the particular judge thinks.

kp.k: Litigation economics limit remedies for ordinary privacy victims
kp.d: Solove presents Hulk Hogan's successful privacy suit as a rare celebrity example supported by substantial litigation resources. He argues that ordinary people may possess stronger substantive privacy claims than celebrities but lack resources to litigate. As technology lets individuals record and distribute private material, defendants' limited assets can make cases unattractive to lawyers, creating a practical enforcement gap even where a legal remedy exists.
qs: The challenge for a private individual is that they don't have the same resources that Hulk Hogan has to bring the suit.
if you're just suing some blogger who has no money, what lawyer is going to spend the time to bring the suit if they're not going to be able to make any money if they win?
Now Jim at the bar can do that, but Jim at the bar doesn't have a big bank account.

kp.k: Law should direct privacy-protective technology design
kp.d: Solove recommends legally mandated recording indicators and suggests, speculatively, technology that could prevent an individual's image from being captured. He distinguishes the latter proposal from currently available capabilities. Drawing analogies to seat belts, airbags and child-resistant medicine packaging, he argues that regulation can make technology embody societal values that profit incentives alone will not reliably deliver.
qs: I think maybe the law should mandate that there be a light or some indication that people are being recorded.
But right now, we don't have that technology, even though I think it's probably possible to have it.
if we don't have the law directing the way technology develops, technology is going to develop in the way that suits the companies that make it.

kp.k: Recording restrictions must preserve accountability for government conduct
kp.d: Solove supports some uses of all-party consent requirements but reports their misuse against people recording police misconduct. He notes that some courts have treated such enforcement as violating the First Amendment and recommends explicit exceptions for recording government officials in relevant contexts. His position is contextual rather than a blanket endorsement or rejection of nonconsensual recording.
qs: some courts have said that's a violation of the First Amendment. So they struck it down.
these are not laws to shield the government from accountability.

It's hard to come up with a one-size-fits-all rule that anytime you record something, like a conversation or an activity or anything else that without someone's consent, that it's always a privacy violation or always something that should be prohibited.

kp.k: AI summaries do not eliminate information-gathering legal issues
kp.d: Asked whether AI-generated call notes without a saved transcript could bypass consent requirements, Solove answers conditionally by distinguishing restrictions on gathering information from restrictions on disclosure; he does not definitively resolve that technical scenario. He explains that keeping an unlawful recording private may still violate applicable law. He also distinguishes federal one-party consent from some states' all-party requirements and emphasizes that interception method can matter independently of Fourth Amendment privacy expectations.
qs: some of the laws will restrict information gathering no matter how it's used. So you don't need a disclosure.
there's a violation for gathering it. Then there's a violation for disclosing it and they're two separate things.
some require all-party consent and the federal law just requires the consent of one party.

kp.k: Fragmented protections complicate advice about apps and wearables
kp.d: Solove argues that assessing privacy protection requires examining jurisdiction, data type, collector, storage, sharing and government access. He contrasts stronger protection for health information held by doctors with more variable protection in apps, illustrating why neither consumers nor an expert can answer broad safety questions without detailed facts. He recommends protective defaults, data minimization, limits on retention and strict restrictions on government access.
qs: If your doctor has it, you have greater protections, it's going to trigger HIPAA. If it's health information in an app, that gets a lot less protection and depends on the privacy notice.

There's so many different variables and questions that have to be asked that it's really hard for an individual to, you know, figure out exactly what the risks are and the implications are to the use of this data.
the company shouldn't have the information if they don't need it, and they shouldn't be storing it forever.
there should be very strict restrictions on government access to this information.

kp.k: Reasonable privacy desires should replace technologically eroding expectations
kp.d: Solove proposes grounding legal intervention in a reasonable desire for privacy rather than expectations that surveillance technology itself diminishes. In discussing satellite surveillance and digitally exposed home activity, he argues for restrictions on collection and use to preserve autonomy and space to live without continual scrutiny. His electronic-fishbowl scenario is a warning about the direction of technology, not an empirical finding that universal surveillance already exists.
qs: expectations are the wrong thing to look at, because technology will constantly change and erode expectations.
whenever there's a reasonable desire for privacy, that's when the law should step in
the law needs to provide people with that space to be themselves and to not be forced to live in an electronic fishbowl.

kp.k: Security benefits require contextual assessment, not blanket technology bans
kp.d: Solove recognizes beneficial recording and crime-prevention uses, including government accountability. He distinguishes technologies with weak security benefits and substantial privacy costs, clearly beneficial less-invasive uses, and genuinely difficult trade-offs. He recommends testing claimed benefits, considering less-invasive alternatives, redesigning systems and using judicial oversight where sufficient, while criticizing absolutist debate. These are policy recommendations rather than evaluated intervention results.
qs: I'm not one who thinks, okay, we just ban all the technology.
Are there alternatives to achieve the same goal that don't have the privacy trade-offs?
Maybe they could be redesigned in certain ways to protect privacy. Maybe with the proper judicial oversight, that might be sufficient to provide the protections.
there really are solutions to be had.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Daniel Solove argues that AI intensifies privacy risks by enabling sensitive inference, scalable surveillance and identification, while existing legal protections remain inadequate.
pts.d: This is primarily a cross-domain account of privacy and surveillance, not a forecast of legal-service automation. Solove makes several concrete claims: (1) algorithms infer sensitive health, religious and political information from apparently innocuous behaviour; (2) chatbots collect intimate information and can give unsuitable or harmful emotional-support advice; (3) AI removes the human-attention bottleneck in surveillance by monitoring feeds and flagging suspicious patterns for review, making existing cameras more invasive; (4) ubiquitous recording and facial recognition erode everyday obscurity and permit individual tracking and exclusion; and (5) continued technological development threatens a future of near-continuous recording with little private refuge. He argues that narrow notions of secrecy, public exposure and third-party possession leave legal protection poorly adapted to these capabilities. He also identifies a practical enforcement gap: ordinary individuals who record and publish others' lives may lack assets that would make litigation economically worthwhile. His proposed response is stronger restrictions on collection, retention and government access, and privacy-protective design requirements, rather than a blanket ban on technology.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Solove supports his account with legal analysis, illustrative incidents, scholarly references and personal experience, rather than quantitative AI-performance or surveillance-impact evidence.
pts.d: For sensitive inference, Solove recounts the Target pregnancy-prediction story as an algorithmic example; he does not present accuracy measurements or establish it as evidence about current generative models. For identification and exclusion, he cites lawyers involved in litigation against what he recalls as Madison Square Garden being excluded using facial recognition. For legal inadequacy, he discusses the third-party doctrine, Jones, Carpenter, privacy torts and federal/state wiretap protections. These are his interpretations of the law, not independent determinations supplied by the analysis. He refers to reports of government purchases of brokered location data and his article Privacy in Authoritarian Times to support the relationship between commercial and government surveillance. He invokes Woodrow Hartzog and Evan Selinger's work on obscurity. He cites the Hulk Hogan litigation to illustrate privacy remedies and litigation resources, then reasons that suing an impecunious individual is commercially unattractive to lawyers. His chatbot observations draw partly on trying the tools, without naming studies or documenting particular harmful-advice incidents. The transcript provides no datasets, model benchmarks, measured surveillance-cost reductions or quantified forecasts.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Solove describes present capabilities and legal gaps in the 2025 interview, alongside undated, conditional predictions of increasingly pervasive surveillance.
pts.d: Sensitive inference, automated surveillance analysis, facial recognition and commercially available personal data are presented as current developments. Near-universal audio/video recording is a directional future prediction, with no deployment date or probability. Its continuation is linked to inadequate legal intervention and profit-driven technology development. Solove repeatedly qualifies legal exposure by jurisdiction, context, the information collected, who holds it, how it is obtained and whether it is disclosed. He says many, not all, laws fail to protect publicly available information. In responding to AI-generated call summaries without a retained transcript, he offers a conditional distinction between unlawful gathering and disclosure, rather than establishing a universal rule that summaries are permitted or prohibited. He acknowledges legitimate safety and accountability uses, possible redesign and judicial oversight, and harder cases requiring trade-offs. Recording indicators are a proposed legal mandate; a personal technology that blocks others from recording someone is explicitly speculative.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected group is the public; governments and businesses gain surveillance capabilities, while individuals face privacy losses, uncertain rights and uneven access to remedies.
pts.d: Consumers and bystanders can have purchases, movements, conversations and health-related behaviour recorded, combined and analysed, including information they did not knowingly reveal. Chatbot users seeking therapy or emotional support face both intimate-data exposure and unreliable advice. Individuals may face targeting, harassment, discriminatory exclusion or scrutiny of political beliefs, with autonomy diminished by continual observation. Governments gain access to private-sector data and more efficient monitoring; companies and data brokers collect, infer and monetise information. Lawyers appear directly as targets of facial-recognition exclusion because of litigation against a venue, not as workers being replaced by AI. Ordinary privacy plaintiffs may be unable to secure economically viable representation against low-asset defendants; celebrities face distinct newsworthiness obstacles despite potentially greater litigation resources. Police and legal advisers also confront uncertain warrant requirements and fragmented rules. Solove places the burden of reform on courts, legislators and technology producers rather than expecting consumers to become AI and privacy-law experts.
